passage: Every Saturday Kamal and Gopika taught English and maths to children of the construction workers behind their school, under a tin shed the site manager let them use. This Saturday, the rain came down so hard the shed roof began to drip onto the chalk slates. Twelve kids and nowhere dry. Gopika wanted to cancel. Kamal looked at the children huddled together, a few still in wet uniforms. "They walked here in this," he said. They borrowed a tarp from the watchman, tied it over the leaking corner, and moved everyone to the dry side. Kamal taught fractions by splitting rotis a mother had sent. When one girl said her old school teacher had called her "dirty", Kamal quietly told her, "Here, you're our best maths student."

qa.q: What did Kamal use to teach fractions?
qa.a: He used rotis a mother had sent.

qa.q: Why did Kamal refuse to cancel even though the shed was leaking?
qa.a: He felt responsible to the children, who had walked through the rain to come, and he did not want to let them down.

qa.q: What did Kamal do well when the girl mentioned being called dirty?
qa.a: He quietly countered the insult with respect, naming her strength so she felt valued rather than judged.

qa.q: How might Gopika's view have changed after the rainy session?
qa.a: She first wanted to cancel, but seeing the tarp work and the children learning may have shown her how much showing up matters.

grounding: Shows teens devoting weekends to a cause and standing up for marginalised children despite a practical obstacle.

passage: When Saurabh joined Class 10 on a scholarship, the others noticed his old shoes and the way he took the bus from the far end of the city. At lunch he ate alone near the water cooler. Kiran noticed too. At first she did nothing. Then one day she overheard two boys calling him "charity case". Her face burned. That afternoon she carried her tiffin to the water cooler and asked Saurabh about the chess book he was reading. By Friday, three more friends were eating there. Kiran also signed up for Sunday mornings at the community kitchen near the railway station, where she stirred huge pots of khichdi. Her mother asked why. "Because I'm tired of just noticing things," Kiran said, stirring harder.

qa.q: Where did Kiran volunteer on Sunday mornings?
qa.a: At the community kitchen near the railway station.

qa.q: What made Kiran decide to act instead of just noticing?
qa.a: Hearing the boys call Saurabh a charity case made her angry and ashamed of doing nothing, so she felt she had to step in.

qa.q: How could a class teacher support what Kiran began?
qa.a: The teacher could arrange mixed seating or group work so Saurabh is included naturally, and speak to the boys about the name-calling.

qa.q: What is it like for Saurabh when Kiran sits with him?
qa.a: After eating alone and being mocked, having someone ask about his chess book likely makes him feel seen as a person, not a label.

grounding: Shows a teen turning concern into action through volunteering and including an excluded classmate.

passage:
"Amma, Irfan and I want to start a petition."
"For what now?"
"A ramp. Nisha from our class uses a wheelchair and she has to wait for two boys to lift her up the science block stairs."
"Doesn't the school know?"
"They say there's no budget. Irfan found the board rules. Schools are meant to be accessible."
"And your exams?"
"Amma, it's one hour a day. Irfan's making the form, I'm getting signatures."
Irfan, from the doorway: "Aunty, we asked Nisha first. She wants it. We're not doing it for her without asking."
"Hmm. That's sensible." A pause. "Lakshmi, don't be rude to the principal."
"I'll be polite. Promise."
"Fine. Give me the form. I'll sign too."

qa.q: Why does Nisha have to wait at the science block?
qa.a: She uses a wheelchair and has to wait for two boys to lift her up the stairs.

qa.q: What might Amma be worried about at first?
qa.a: She seems worried the petition will eat into Lakshmi's exam preparation and that Lakshmi may be rude to the principal.

qa.q: Which choice by Irfan and Lakshmi was especially wise, and why?
qa.a: Asking Nisha first made sure they were supporting what she actually wanted, rather than speaking over her.

qa.q: What would change if they had started without talking to Nisha?
qa.a: The campaign might embarrass her or not match her needs, and she could feel like a project instead of a classmate.

grounding: Shows teens committing to a cause for a marginalised peer and convincing a parent while balancing studies.

passage: Last year I thought volunteering meant weekend photos at a tree-planting drive. Then I noticed that Manoj, who uses a wheelchair, never came to library period. The library was on the second floor, and our school has no lift. Everyone knew; nobody did anything, including me, for two years. I asked him if he minded me raising it. He said, 'Go ahead, Ankita, but don't make me a poster.' So I didn't. I got twenty classmates to sign a request, met the principal with Manoj, and we offered to run a book trolley on the ground floor every Wednesday ourselves. It's been eight months. I still run it. What changed in me is that I stopped looking for causes far away.

qa.q: Which floor was the library on?
qa.a: The second floor.

qa.q: What did Manoj mean by 'don't make me a poster'?
qa.a: He wanted the problem fixed without being turned into a symbol or pity story; he cared about his dignity.

qa.q: What did Ankita get right in taking up the issue?
qa.a: Ankita asked Manoj first, respected his wish, and offered practical help instead of only complaining.

qa.q: How might other students benefit from the trolley?
qa.a: They also get easy access to books on the ground floor, and see that small changes can include everyone.

grounding: Shows a teenager directing their energy into service by standing up for a classmate who was being left out.

passage: Volunteer coordinator's note, Sunday community kitchen, week six. Zubin arrived early again, before the dal was on. He has stopped asking what to do and now checks the rota himself. Today an elderly man was turned away at the gate by another volunteer because he had no token. Zubin went after him, brought him back, and asked me quietly whether we could keep five extra plates for people without tokens. Yusuf, who helps with serving, backed him up. Zubin was polite but firm. I agreed to try it for a month. Next step: I will ask Zubin and Yusuf to write the new rule on the board and explain it to the other volunteers themselves, so it doesn't feel like a favour.

qa.q: How many extra plates did Zubin ask to keep?
qa.a: Five extra plates.

qa.q: Why did Zubin go after the elderly man?
qa.a: He seemed troubled that someone in need was turned away over a token, and wanted to fix it rather than just feel bad.

qa.q: Why is asking the boys to explain the new rule a good step?
qa.a: It gives them ownership and helps other volunteers understand the reason instead of seeing it as special treatment.

qa.q: How might the volunteer who turned the man away feel?
qa.a: Perhaps embarrassed or defensive, since they were following the token rule; a clear explanation may help them accept the change.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager committed to volunteering who speaks up for people left out by a rule, seen by a coordinator.

passage:
Reena's diary, Saturday
Third week of teaching the kids at the community hall. They're children of the construction workers building the tower next door, and most have never had a proper notebook. Omkar and I brought chart paper and crayons. Today a boy, maybe eight, read a whole sentence alone and looked at me like he'd climbed a mountain. On the way out, a guy from our class passed and said, "Doing charity for selfies?" Omkar laughed it off. I didn't. I told him the kids have names, and they deserve better than jokes. He went quiet. I'm tired, but I've never felt more useful.

qa.q: What did Reena and Omkar bring?
qa.a: Chart paper and crayons.

qa.q: How did Reena feel after the boy read his first sentence?
qa.a: Reena felt proud and deeply useful, moved by his achievement.

qa.q: What would you advise Reena about the classmate's comment?
qa.a: Stay calm and keep the focus on the children, as Reena did, without getting drawn into an argument.

qa.q: How might the boy who read the sentence see the Saturday classes?
qa.a: As a place where he feels capable and seen.

grounding: Shows a teenager committing energy to volunteering and standing up for marginalised children.

passage:
Zubin: did you see Arya had to wait outside the science lab again?
Hemant: yeah. the lift was broken and her wheelchair can't do stairs
Zubin: third time this month 😠
Hemant: it's not fair. she misses every practical
Zubin: let's do something
Hemant: like what?
Zubin: petition to the principal. ramp or ground-floor lab
Hemant: i'll draft it. you get signatures?
Zubin: done. i'll ask Arya first if she wants us to
Hemant: good call. it's her thing, not ours
Zubin: she said yes 👍 she's coming with us to the office
Hemant: tomorrow after assembly then

qa.q: Why did Arya have to wait outside the lab?
qa.a: The lift was broken and her wheelchair can't do stairs.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel about Arya waiting outside again?
qa.a: Angry and frustrated at the unfairness of it happening so often.

qa.q: What did the boys get right in their plan?
qa.a: They asked Arya first and included her, so the campaign respected her voice.

qa.q: How might Arya feel when they ask her first?
qa.a: Respected and supported, since it's her need and her choice.

grounding: Shows teenagers channelling energy into a civic cause for a classmate who uses a wheelchair.

passage: In the small town, the ration office was always crowded with elderly people who couldn't read the forms. Chetan, seventeen, started going there on Saturdays with a pen and a folding stool, filling forms for anyone who asked. His classmate Tenzin, whose family came from a Tibetan settlement nearby, joined him. One Saturday a man in the queue told Tenzin, "Outsiders shouldn't be helping here." Chetan put down his pen. "He was born two streets away, uncle. Same as me." The man grumbled but let Tenzin fill his form. Afterwards Tenzin said, "You didn't have to." Chetan shrugged. "Yes, I did."

qa.q: What did Chetan bring to the ration office?
qa.a: A pen and a folding stool.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when he put down his pen?
qa.a: He felt protective and indignant at the unfair remark about Tenzin.

qa.q: What made Chetan's response effective?
qa.a: He corrected the man calmly with a fact, without insulting him, and kept helping.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel after Chetan stood up for him?
qa.a: Grateful and supported, though perhaps still hurt by the remark.

grounding: Shows a teenager volunteering at a public office and standing up for a classmate treated as an outsider.

passage: In Malmö, the new boy, Yosef, had arrived from Syria in September and still spoke little Swedish. Some of the class mimicked his accent. Lars, sixteen, had laughed once, then felt uncomfortable about it for days. In October he asked his teacher if he could start a homework club at the library on Wednesdays, open to anyone learning Swedish. Four students came the first week, including Yosef. Lars explained grammar badly and Yosef corrected his maths. When a classmate sneered at them in the corridor, Lars said, "He's in my club. Leave it." His voice wobbled, but he held his ground. By December, twelve students came every week, and Lars had given up two afternoons of football for it.

qa.q: On which day did the homework club meet?
qa.a: On Wednesdays.

qa.q: How did Lars feel after laughing at Yosef once?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and guilty for days.

qa.q: What was effective about Lars's response, and how could the school support it?
qa.a: He turned his guilt into a club that helped many students; the school could give the club a teacher and a regular room.

qa.q: How might Yosef see the club and Lars's defence in the corridor?
qa.a: Yosef likely feels welcomed and less alone, with a place where his skills are valued.

grounding: A Swedish teenager starts a homework club for newcomer students and stands up for a mocked classmate.

passage: At the community centre in Dharavi, Joseph, seventeen, arrived every Saturday at nine to teach reading to a group of eight-year-olds. The coordinator, Tejas, had warned him the kids were restless. The first week, they ignored him. The second week, a boy threw a book. Joseph went home frustrated and nearly quit. But he came back with picture cards and let each child choose a story. By week five, the kids were waiting at the door. One girl read a whole page aloud and looked at him, beaming. Joseph felt a warmth in his chest he couldn't explain. "I'll take the Tuesday group too," he told Tejas. "If you need someone."

qa.q: At what time did Joseph arrive every Saturday?
qa.a: At nine.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel after the second week?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and discouraged, nearly quitting.

qa.q: What change helped Joseph connect with the children?
qa.a: Bringing picture cards and letting each child choose a story.

qa.q: How might Tejas see Joseph offering to take the Tuesday group too?
qa.a: Tejas would likely be pleased and grateful to have such a committed volunteer.

grounding: A teenager finds meaning in volunteering to teach reading at a community centre despite a rough start.

passage:
Dear Tanuja Ma'am,
I am Nazia from Class 10B. I am writing about Mehul in our class, who uses a wheelchair. Every day he has to wait for two peons to carry him up to our classroom on the first floor. He jokes about it, but I have seen his face when everyone is watching. He also cannot go to the library or the lab with us. I have talked to twenty-three students, and all of them signed the attached page. We are asking for a ramp at the side entrance, and for our class to be moved to the ground floor until then. Some of us are ready to help raise funds at the Annual Day stall. Please let us meet you this week.
Respectfully,
Nazia

qa.q: How many students signed the page?
qa.a: Twenty-three students.

qa.q: What does Nazia seem to feel about Mehul's situation?
qa.a: Nazia seems concerned and upset about the unfairness, noticing Mehul's face when others are watching.

qa.q: What makes Nazia's letter a strong way to push for change?
qa.a: It is respectful, gives specific facts, shows support from classmates and proposes clear, practical steps.

qa.q: How might Mehul feel about the letter?
qa.a: He may feel supported and grateful, though maybe a little self-conscious about being the subject of it.

grounding: A teenager writes to the principal on behalf of a classmate who uses a wheelchair, asking for a ramp.

passage:
You want to know how I started the blanket drive, Vaibhav? It wasn't planned.
I'm Irfan. Last December I was walking back from tuition and saw a family sleeping under the flyover, kids with no socks. I kept walking. That night I couldn't stop seeing their feet.
So I asked my building's group if anyone had old blankets. Three people replied. Then my mother made me go door to door. Terrible. Knocking on aunties' doors. But we got forty blankets.
We took them with the local shelter's volunteers, not on our own. The shelter manager said what people actually needed was socks and rice more than blankets. That taught me something.
This year I'm asking the shelter first what they need. Then we collect.

qa.q: How many blankets did they collect?
qa.a: Forty blankets.

qa.q: How did Irfan feel after walking past the family?
qa.a: Irfan felt uneasy and guilty, unable to stop seeing the children's feet that night.

qa.q: What did Irfan learn about helping well?
qa.a: To ask the shelter what people need first, instead of guessing, and to go with the shelter's volunteers.

qa.q: What might the shelter manager feel about young volunteers like Irfan?
qa.a: The manager may feel grateful and glad to guide eager helpers toward what really helps.

grounding: A teen describes turning discomfort about homelessness into a considered volunteer effort.

passage:
I'm Kalyani, Gurpreet's classmate. Since the monsoon, she has been different.
It started when a boy in our class who uses a wheelchair couldn't get to the new science lab on the second floor. Everyone felt bad for a day. Gurpreet didn't stop at a day.
She wrote a letter to the principal and got twenty signatures. When nothing happened, she measured the stairs, found out about ramps, and presented to the school council with photos.
Some people called her a show-off. She kept going, quietly. I don't know if she's doing it for him or for herself or both.
Last week the school moved his class's labs to the ground floor. Gurpreet just said, "Good," and went back to her book. But she was smiling at the page.

qa.q: How many signatures did Gurpreet get?
qa.a: Twenty signatures.

qa.q: What does Gurpreet smiling at her book suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt quietly satisfied and relieved that the change finally happened.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet do that made her effort work?
qa.a: She kept going after the first letter failed, gathered facts and photos, and used the school council.

qa.q: How does Kalyani see Gurpreet's campaign?
qa.a: Kalyani admires the persistence but admits she isn't sure of Gurpreet's reasons.

grounding: A classmate observes a teen campaign steadily for a peer who uses a wheelchair.

passage:
First Saturday: Kishore joined the neighbourhood reading circle for younger kids only because his mother pushed him. He sat at the back of the community hall, bored, while Minakshi didi read to eight children.
Two weeks later: one small boy, who spoke mostly Bhojpuri and was teased for it, wouldn't read aloud. Kishore, whose grandmother spoke Bhojpuri, sat beside him and whispered the words in both languages. The boy read a whole page. The others clapped.
A month on: Kishore arrived early, arranged the mats, and asked Minakshi didi if they could add books in other languages. "Some of these kids are made to feel small for how they talk at home," he said. "Not here." He brought three books from his grandmother's shelf.

qa.q: What did Kishore bring from his grandmother's shelf?
qa.a: Three books.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel at the first Saturday?
qa.a: He felt bored and reluctant, sitting at the back only because his mother pushed him.

qa.q: How could Minakshi didi support Kishore's new commitment?
qa.a: She could give him a regular role, like helping kids who speak other languages, and include his book ideas.

qa.q: How might the small boy feel after reading a whole page?
qa.a: He likely felt proud and accepted, especially after being teased for how he talks.

grounding: Shows a teen's service growing from reluctance into standing up for a marginalised child.

passage: Jomon, you asked why old Sahil Sir still teaches at the night school after office. At sixteen I was at a good school in Pune, and there was a boy, Gopal, whose fees were paid by a trust. The others called him "charity case" and hid his books. One day I said, loudly, "His marks are better than yours." That cost me a few friends. Gopal told me the kids in his basti had no one to help with homework. So every Saturday I went there with two friends and a blackboard propped on bricks. Twelve children came the first week. By the monsoon, forty. My father thought I was wasting study time, until Gopal's sister topped her class. That blackboard is still in my office.

qa.q: How many children came the first week?
qa.a: Twelve children came the first week.

qa.q: How did young Sahil feel after speaking up for Gopal and losing friends?
qa.a: He probably felt lonely for a while, but also sure and determined that it was the right thing.

qa.q: What choice turned Sahil's defence of Gopal into a lasting mission?
qa.a: Listening when Gopal described the basti children's need, then going every Saturday with a blackboard, turned one stand into ongoing service.

qa.q: How did Sahil's father see the Saturday classes at first?
qa.a: His father thought they were wasting study time, until Gopal's sister topped her class.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager defending a marginalised classmate and turning it into volunteer teaching, told by a senior colleague.
